title: Jacobian Diagnostics for Under-Constrained Zero-Knowledge Circuits
abstract:
Under-constrained arithmetic circuits are a recurring source of soundness failures in zero-knowledge applications: after fixing the public statement, a malicious prover may be able to assign a security-relevant wire in more than one way while still satisfying the circuit.  Existing tools attack this uniqueness question with solver-based checking, direct polynomial solving, abstract interpretation, or fuzzing.  We study a complementary algebraic diagnostic based on exact Jacobian linear algebra.

The method separates three notions that are often conflated: first-order rigidity at a sampled witness, finite algebraic dependence on an irreducible component, and uniqueness over the circuit field.  At a satisfying assignment, the kernel of the constraint Jacobian augmented with rows fixing the statement coordinates is the Zariski tangent space of the corresponding fibre scheme, so motion of a target coordinate in this kernel certifies infinitesimal freedom at that witness. Under suitable separability hypotheses, the associated differential representation also recovers
component-wise algebraic dependence, while a certified triangular degree calculus provides multiplicity bounds for locally rigid targets.  An exact sparse implementation handles \texttt{gnark} R1CS instances in the $6$k--$60$k-constraint range in preliminary measurements, and a checkable degree budget ($m<\log_2 p$ quadratic constraints) discharges the separability hypothesis at gadget scale.

The principal limitation is witness locality: a circuit may appear rigid at an honest witness while becoming under-constrained on a prover-reachable degenerate branch.  In a measured $2{,}396$-constraint \texttt{gnark}~0.14.0 scalar-multiplication gadget, an honest witness exposed no free target wires while a degenerate adversarial witness exposed five.  We therefore position Jacobian analysis as a scalable candidate detector and localisation tool, to be combined with adversarial
witness generation and solver- or certificate-based confirmation.

Jacobian Diagnostics for Under-Constrained Zero-Knowledge
                               Circuits
                                          Vijaykumar Singh


                                                Abstract
         Under-constrained arithmetic circuits are a recurring source of soundness failures in zero-
     knowledge applications: after fixing the public statement, a malicious prover may be able to
     assign a security-relevant wire in more than one way while still satisfying the circuit. Existing
     tools attack this uniqueness question with solver-based checking, direct polynomial solving,
     abstract interpretation, or fuzzing. We study a complementary algebraic diagnostic based on
     exact Jacobian linear algebra.
         The method separates three notions that are often conflated: first-order rigidity at a sampled
     witness, finite algebraic dependence on an irreducible component, and uniqueness over the cir-
     cuit field. At a satisfying assignment, the kernel of the constraint Jacobian augmented with rows
     fixing the statement coordinates is the Zariski tangent space of the corresponding fibre scheme,
     so motion of a target coordinate in this kernel certifies infinitesimal freedom at that witness.
     Under suitable separability hypotheses, the associated differential representation also recovers
     component-wise algebraic dependence, while a certified triangular degree calculus provides mul-
     tiplicity bounds for locally rigid targets. An exact sparse implementation handles gnark R1CS
     instances in the 6k–60k-constraint range in preliminary measurements, and a checkable degree
     budget (m < log2 p quadratic constraints) discharges the separability hypothesis at gadget scale.
         The principal limitation is witness locality: a circuit may appear rigid at an honest witness
     while becoming under-constrained on a prover-reachable degenerate branch. In a measured
     2,396-constraint gnark 0.14.0 scalar-multiplication gadget, an honest witness exposed no free
     target wires while a degenerate adversarial witness exposed five. We therefore position Jacobian
     analysis as a scalable candidate detector and localisation tool, to be combined with adversarial
     witness generation and solver- or certificate-based confirmation.


1   Introduction
Arithmetic-circuit proof systems separate two questions that are easy to confuse. The cryptographic
proof system establishes that the prover knows an assignment satisfying a relation. The circuit
author must separately ensure that this relation is the intended one. If a witness, intermediate
value, or output that should be fixed by the statement is not suﬀiciently constrained, a prover
may satisfy the circuit with an unintended assignment. Such bugs are generally referred to as
under-constraint bugs.
    A standard formalisation asks whether designated outputs are uniquely determined by the public
inputs. Picus/QED2 checks this property using lightweight uniqueness propagation followed by
SMT reasoning and can return either a proof of uniqueness, a counterexample pair, or unknown [1].
Related work uses abstract interpretation and SMT for Halo2 circuits [2], while AC4 encodes circuit
constraints as polynomial equations and applies computer-algebraic solving techniques [4]. zkFuzz
addresses a broader semantic property—Trace-Constraint Consistency—and uses mutation-based
fuzzing to search for both under- and over-constrained behaviour, including discrepancies involving
intermediate computations and program aborts [5]. These approaches cover different parts of the

                                                     1
design space: global uniqueness reasoning can be expensive, direct algebraic solving can suffer from
polynomial-system complexity, and fuzzing trades proof for search.
    This paper investigates a different primitive: exact Jacobian linear algebra over the circuit field.
The motivation is classical. Jacobians represent algebraic independence in characteristic zero and,
under suitable degree or separability assumptions, in suﬀiciently large positive characteristic [7,
8, 9]. The corresponding dependence structure is an algebraic matroid [6]. R1CS constraints
are quadratic, highly sparse, and usually defined over prime fields of cryptographic size. These
properties make Jacobian computations inexpensive compared with general polynomial elimination.
    The central point, however, is not merely that a Jacobian can be computed. The relevant
question is what its rank actually proves. A single pointwise Jacobian does not decide global
uniqueness. It answers a local differential question. The algebraic-matroid interpretation answers
a generic algebraic-dependence question on an irreducible component. Actual under-constraint is
normally a finite-field uniqueness question. These are related but distinct properties.

Contributions. This paper makes the following contributions.

1. A precise algebraic formulation. We distinguish uniqueness over Fp , algebraic dependence
   on an irreducible component, and first-order rigidity at a witness. Algebraic-matroid closure
   corresponds to finite algebraic dependence, not uniqueness.

2. A pointwise Jacobian diagnostic for R1CS. For a satisfying witness a, the kernel of
   the constraint Jacobian augmented with rows fixing the conditioned coordinates is exactly the
   tangent space of the corresponding fibre at a. A nonzero target coordinate in that kernel is a
   direct certificate of infinitesimal freedom at the sampled witness.

3. An exact sparse implementation at realistic circuit sizes. The current implementa-
   tion exports a satisfying gnark witness, assembles the sparse Jacobian over Fp , and computes
   rank/nullspace information using exact sparse elimination. Preliminary measurements on the
   current corpus reach 6k–60k constraints and show roughly 500–1000× improvements over the
   dense prototype on the tested instances.

4. A checkable separability certificate at gadget scale. If an analysed subsystem contains
   m quadratic constraints with 2m < p, every irreducible component has degree < p, which
   forces the relevant coordinate-field extensions to be separably generated. This discharges the
   separability hypothesis for component-wise differential closure, but not the characteristic-free
   pointwise caveats.

5. A restricted but sound multiplicity calculus. We give a product-of-degrees bound for
   triangularly certified subcircuits. This refines a first-order “rigid” verdict into a finite ambiguity
   bound when the required structural preconditions hold. We also explain why a blanket 2q rule
   for arbitrary R1CS cones would be unsound.

6. A concrete witness-locality failure mode. A real hint-based defect is invisible at the
   library’s honest witness and visible at a degenerate adversarial witness. This shows that case
   analysis is not eliminated; for conditional gadgets it moves from symbolic constraint reasoning
   into the choice of witnesses at which the Jacobian is evaluated.

7. A public soundness benchmark and an applicability taxonomy. We classify the eleven
   issues of a critical gnark advisory into continuous (first-order) freedom, finite/discrete ambiguity,
   semantic omission absent from the encoded relation, and one out-of-scope completeness bug,


                                                   2
      and confirm on the actual implementation that the diagnostic catches the first class and, by
      design, not the others. The taxonomy of misses delimits the method’s scope as sharply as the
      hits establish its reach.

    The intended role of the method is therefore specific, and stating it precisely is part of the
contribution. Jacobian diagnostics eﬀiciently detect infinitesimal under-determination in large
arithmetic circuits and localise the responsible variables; finite (discrete) ambiguity and semantic
omissions require complementary methods. The value is a two-stage pipeline,
               cheap Jacobian                                  solver / manual / certificate
large R1CS −−−−−−−−−−→ small suspicious region −−−−−−−−−−−−−−−−−−→ security conclusion,

in which the diagnostic is a high-throughput first stage, not a complete decision procedure. A first-
order-free verdict is a strong, exact local signal that prioritises the responsible cone; a rigid verdict
does not establish safety, because discrete alternatives may still exist; and if the intended semantics
are not encoded in the constraint system at all, no analysis of that relation alone can recover the
missing condition. The misses are as informative as the hits: they tell the auditor exactly when
not to trust a rigid verdict.


2      Circuit model and security property
2.1     R1CS as a polynomial system
Let k = Fp and let x = (x1 , . . . , xn ). An R1CS instance consists of constraints

                                (Li · x)(Ri · x) − (Oi · x) = 0,       i = 1, . . . , m,                     (1)

where Li , Ri , Oi are aﬀine or homogeneous linear forms, depending on the chosen encoding. A
constant-one wire can be fixed to 1 or eliminated before analysis. Write

                fi (x) = (Li · x)(Ri · x) − (Oi · x),        I = (f1 , . . . , fm ) ⊆ k[x1 , . . . , xn ].

The satisfying assignments are

                                 Vk (I) = {a ∈ k n : f1 (a) = · · · = fm (a) = 0}.

For geometric statements we use the algebraic closure Fp and distinguish the R1CS scheme from
its reduced irreducible components when necessary.
    Let P denote the genuinely public coordinates. For a particular analysis let F ⊇ P be the
coordinates whose values are conditioned on. In a whole-circuit security query, F contains P
together with structural constants such as the constant-one coordinate. A sliced analysis may
additionally fix boundary coordinates, but conclusions from such a slice are conditional on those
extra values. For u ∈ k F , let Vu be the fibre scheme cut out by

                                           Ju = I + (xi − ui : i ∈ F ),

and write
                                         Vu (k) = {a ∈ Vk (I) : aF = u}.                                     (2)
Let T be the security-relevant target coordinates. Internal nondeterminism is not necessarily a
security bug if it cannot affect a semantic value checked by the application, so T should be derived
from the intended relation.

                                                         3
Threat model. The adversary is a malicious prover. Apart from coordinates fixed by the state-
ment and structural constants, it controls every witness, hint, and advice coordinate. The verifier
enforces the R1CS equations, not the honest witness-generation procedure. A satisfiable degenerate
branch is therefore prover-reachable even if honest tooling never selects it.

Definition 1 (Finite-field uniqueness). For a whole-circuit security query, take F to contain only
the public statement and structural constants. A target xj , j ∈ T , is uniquely determined by the
statement u if {aj : a ∈ Vu (k)} has at most one element. It is non-unique if there exist a, b ∈ Vu (k)
with aj ̸= bj .

    A pair (a, b) agreeing on F and differing on a target is the most direct certificate of non-
uniqueness for this property. Solver-based tools such as Picus are designed around this kind of
relational query [1].

2.2   Three notions of determination
The analysis uses two weaker notions, both useful but neither equivalent to finite-field uniqueness.

Definition 2 (Component-wise algebraic dependence). Let C be a reduced irreducible component
with prime ideal p and function field K(C). The coordinate xj is algebraic over the fixed coordinates
on C if its image in K(C) is algebraic over Fp (xi : i ∈ F ).

    This is the closure relation in the algebraic matroid associated with C. It says that generically
on that component, fixing F leaves finitely many possibilities for xj ; it does not say there is exactly
one.

Definition 3 (First-order rigidity at a witness). Let a ∈ Vu (k). A target xj is first-order rigid at
a relative to F if every Zariski tangent vector to the fibre scheme Vu at a has zero jth coordinate.
Otherwise it is infinitesimally free at a.

   These three notions are not a hierarchy. Finite-field uniqueness, component-wise algebraic
dependence, and pointwise first-order rigidity can disagree in either direction without additional
hypotheses. Section 5 gives explicit counterexamples.

3.1   Component-wise algebraic matroids
An algebraic matroid is naturally attached to a field extension, equivalently to a prime ideal. This
component-wise qualification matters because an R1CS ideal need not be prime, radical, or equidi-
mensional. Let C be a reduced irreducible component with function field K = K(C). For a
coordinate set S,

is algebraic of degree two over x.

3.2   Differentials and generic Jacobian representations
For a prime component C with function field K, consider

In positive characteristic, ordinary differentials represent algebraic dependence only when the rele-
vant extensions are separably generated [7, 9, 10].

Proposition 5 (Generic differential closure). Let C be a reduced irreducible component. Suppose
K(C) is separably generated over both Fp (xi : i ∈ F ) and Fp (xi : i ∈ F ∪ {j}). Then

                         xj ∈ clC (F )    ⇐⇒       dxj ∈ spanK(C) {dxi : i ∈ F }.

At a generic smooth point of C, this dependence can be read from a Jacobian of local equations that
define the reduced component scheme-theoretically near that point.

Proof sketch. For S ∈ {F, F ∪ {j}} put LS = Fp (xi : i ∈ S). Under separable generation, the
natural map
                               ΩLS /Fp ⊗LS K(C) −→ ΩK(C)/Fp
is injective, and the span of {dxi : i ∈ S} has dimension trdegFp LS . Thus adjoining xj raises
transcendence degree exactly when adjoining dxj raises differential rank. At a smooth point, the
conormal space of the reduced component is the row span of a Jacobian of local defining equations.


    Without separability the equivalence can fail in either direction. On C = V (x2 − xp1 ), one has
dx2 = 0 although x2 is transcendental over Fp ; with F = ∅ and target x2 this produces a spurious
“determined” verdict. With F = {x2 } and target x1 , the target is purely inseparably algebraic over
the fixed field while dx1 does not lie in the span of dx2 .
    The relevant large-characteristic criterion must also be stated carefully. For polynomial families
of degree at most δ and transcendence degree r, the classical suﬀicient condition in the Jacobian
criterion of Beecken, Mittmann, and Saxena has exponential form char(k) > δ r [7]. This does not
give a whole-circuit guarantee when r is large. The following component-degree argument instead
gives a checkable certificate on small quadratic dependency cones.

Lemma 6 (Coordinate-projection degree bound). Let C ⊆ AnF be irreducible and let B be a subset

of the coordinate functions forming a transcendence basis of K(C)/Fp . Then

                                         [K(C) : Fp (B)] ≤ deg C.

If deg C < p, this finite extension is separable.

Proof. The coordinate projection πB : C → Adim C is dominant and generically finite. Its generic
scheme-theoretic fibre has length [K(C) : Fp (B)]. Fixing generic values of the coordinates in B
cuts C by dim C aﬀine coordinate hyperplanes, and the resulting zero-dimensional intersection
has length at most deg C. Hence the degree bound. If the field extension were inseparable, its
inseparable degree would be a positive power of p, so p would divide the total degree. Thus total
degree < p forces separability. The converse is false: a separable extension may also have degree
divisible by p.

Proposition 7 (Degree-budget separability certificate). Let C be an irreducible component of the
zero set of m polynomials of degree at most two over Fp . If 2m < p, then K(C) is separably
generated over every coordinate subfield Fp (xi : i ∈ S). Consequently, the separability hypotheses of
Proposition 5 hold for every pair (F, j) on C.

Proof. Bézout’s inequality gives deg C ≤ 2m < p. Fix a coordinate set S and choose a coordinate
transcendence basis B0 ⊆ S of Fp (xi : i ∈ S)/Fp . Extend B0 by matroid exchange to a coordinate
transcendence basis B = B0 ⊔ B1 of K(C)/Fp . By Lemma 6, K(C)/Fp (B) is finite separable.
Because Fp (xi : i ∈ S) is algebraic over Fp (B0 ), B1 remains algebraically independent over Fp (xi :
i ∈ S). After adjoining B1 , the extension to K(C) is an intermediate extension of the separable
algebraic extension K(C)/Fp (B). Thus B1 is a separating transcendence basis over the chosen
coordinate subfield.

Corollary 8 (Quadratic constraint budget). For an analysed subsystem of m quadratic R1CS
constraints with m < log2 p, every irreducible component satisfies the separability hypotheses of
Proposition 5. For a field of roughly 254 bits, m ≤ 253 is a suﬀicient checkable budget.

    This certificate removes only the positive-characteristic inseparability obstruction. It does not
show that the sampled R1CS witness is generic or smooth, that the original R1CS ideal is radical,
that all irreducible components have been sampled, or that no other prover-reachable branch exists.
    The bound cannot be extended to arbitrary circuit scale merely because each R1CS equation
is quadratic. A binary square-and-multiply chain computes z = xp using

                                     ⌊log2 p⌋ + popcount(p) − 1

quadratic multiplication constraints. For a typical 254-bit prime with about half its bits set, this
is roughly 380 constraints; the worst-case binary count is below 2 · 254. The resulting irreducible
curve has z = xp , so dz = 0 although z is transcendental in the function field. This is an explicit
whole-circuit-scale inseparability failure class built entirely from quadratic constraints.

   This formulation allows one row reduction of M (a) to classify many targets.

4.2   What a positive finding means
If the computation returns a tangent vector with a nonzero target coordinate, the result is an exact
statement about the linearisation at the sampled witness. At a smooth point of a positive- dimen-
sional fibre over Fp , such a tangent direction is evidence of genuine local variation. Nevertheless,
the tangent vector itself is not a second Fp witness. A security report should therefore distinguish
 1. infinitesimal freedom: certified by v ∈ ker M (a);

 2. algebraic non-determination on a component: a generic/component-wise statement; and

 3. finite-field non-uniqueness: certified by two actual satisfying assignments.
The Jacobian is most useful as a fast route from a large circuit to a small suspicious slice that can
then be confirmed by direct construction, solving, or manual reasoning.

4.3   Analysis procedure
The implementation follows five steps.
 1. Obtain a satisfying witness. Export the full assignment from the circuit’s witness generator
    and verify independently that every R1CS equation vanishes.

 2. Mark conditioned coordinates. Include the public inputs and structural constants in F .
    For a local slice, record any additionally fixed boundary coordinates explicitly so that the result
    is not mistaken for a global claim.

                                                   7
3. Assemble J(a). Use (3) directly from the sparse R1CS rows. No symbolic expansion of the
   full polynomial system is required.
4. Reduce M (a) over Fp . Compute exact rank and enough nullspace or row-space information
   to classify the requested targets.
5. Trace suspicious coordinates back to the circuit. Rank information by target relevance
   and dependency cone, then confirm security-relevant candidates with an explicit second witness
   or a stronger algebraic certificate when possible.
   The procedure is deliberately witness-parameterised. Section 9 explains why a single honest
witness is insuﬀicient for branch-sensitive gadgets.


5     Small examples
The following examples separate the properties that the analysis must not conflate.

5.1   Bilinear freedom
Consider
                                              Y = XW
with Y fixed. At a witness (X, W, Y ) = (2, 3, 6), the linearised fixed-Y equation is
                                          3 dX + 2 dW = 0.
The kernel contains nonzero directions in both X and W . The fixed-Y fibre is a hyperbola over
the algebraic closure and both coordinates vary. This is the ideal case for the pointwise test: the
tangent freedom reflects genuine positive-dimensional under-determination.

5.2   Guarded freedom without symbolic case splitting
Consider
                                             x(s − 1) = 0
with selector s fixed. At s = 1, the derivative with respect to x is zero and x is infinitesimally free.
At s = 0, the equation becomes −x = 0 and the derivative with respect to x is nonzero. Once
the witness is fixed, the Jacobian handles both cases uniformly as field linear algebra; no symbolic
branch split is required inside the rank computation.
    This observation is useful but limited. If the witness generator always produces s = 0, evaluating
only that witness does not reveal the s = 1 branch. The case split has been moved to witness
selection rather than eliminated globally.

5.3   Finite ambiguity invisible to the tangent test
Consider
                                                w2 = x
with x = 1 and odd characteristic. At either root w = ±1,
                                              2w dw = 0,
so dw = 0. The wire is first-order rigid at each root, but it is not unique: there are two solutions.
Algebraically, w lies in the matroid closure of x because it has degree two over k(x). This is exactly
why algebraic closure must not be described as uniqueness.

                                                   8
5.4   A non-radical false alarm
Consider the single equation
                                                w2 = 0.
Set-theoretically, the only solution is w = 0. However, the derivative vanishes at that point, so
the Jacobian reports a tangent direction in w. The issue is scheme-theoretic multiplicity: the ideal
(w2 ) is non-radical even though its reduced variety is the single point defined by (w).
    This example shows that a rank deficiency can be a false alarm for uniqueness even when there
is no second component and no alternate field point.

5.5   Coupled finite ambiguity
The system
                                        w + u = 5,        wu = 6
has the two solutions (w, u) = (2, 3) and (3, 2) over fields where these values are distinct. Neither
variable needs to appear in a syntactic self-square. Eliminating u = 5 − w gives

                                           w2 − 5w + 6 = 0.

Finite multiplicity is therefore a property of the system and its elimination structure, not of a single
constraint’s surface syntax.

5.6   Uniqueness without algebraic dependence
Let p ≡ 3 (mod 4) and consider x2 + y 2 = 0 with no fixed coordinates and target x. Since −1 is a
quadratic non-residue in Fp , the only Fp -solution is (0, 0), so x is unique over the circuit field. Over
Fp the variety is the union of the two lines y = ±ix, and x is transcendental on each component.
The Jacobian also vanishes at the origin. Geometric freedom does not by itself produce a second
Fp witness.

5.7   Rigidity without algebraic dependence
Consider x = w2 with no fixed coordinates and target x. At (w, x) = (0, 0) the linearised equation is
dx = 0, so x is first-order rigid at that witness. Nevertheless, x is transcendental on the irreducible
parabola and is non-unique over Fp . First-order rigidity at a special witness does not imply algebraic
dependence on the component.


6     Exact sparse linear algebra at circuit scale
6.1   Why sparsity matters
An R1CS Jacobian is large but structurally sparse. Each derivative row is supported only on co-
ordinates occurring in the corresponding linear forms. Dense elimination destroys this advantage
immediately: memory becomes quadratic in the number of wires and arithmetic work grows cubi-
cally in the worst case. The current implementation instead stores rows sparsely and chooses pivots
using a Markowitz-style fill heuristic.
    All arithmetic is exact in Fp . A pivot operation multiplies by a field inverse and eliminates
the pivot column from the remaining sparse rows. The implementation records enough elimination
data to recover rank, free columns, and target-coordinate participation in nullspace directions. A

6.2   Witness extraction from gnark
For the current prototype, satisfying assignments are exported from gnark’s R1CS solver. The
full vector must be aligned with the compiled R1CS wire ordering rather than reconstructed from
source-level variable names. Before any Jacobian analysis, the tool reevaluates every constraint on
the exported vector. This guards against indexing errors in the analysis pipeline itself.
    The Jacobian need not be obtained by symbolic differentiation. Equation (3) can be evaluated
directly from the three sparse R1CS linear forms. This keeps the analysis close to the actual verifier
relation and avoids dependence on source-language simplification.

6.3   Current scale measurements
The present implementation has been exercised on real gnark circuits in the 6k–60k-constraint
range. Preliminary measurements show approximately 500–1000× speedups over the original dense
prototype on the instances tested so far. These are feasibility measurements, not yet a reproducible
benchmark suite: the current draft does not provide per-circuit wire/nonzero counts, hardware,
software commits, peak memory, and wall-clock time. A separate solver-based cone analysis en-
countered a determining cone of roughly 1,179 constraints around a Poseidon/Merkle backbone.
    These measurements establish feasibility of exact Jacobian processing at the relevant size. They
do not establish that the Jacobian is a substitute for solver-based uniqueness checking: the two
tools answer different questions. A complete evaluation should therefore report both throughput
and the rate at which Jacobian candidates can be confirmed as actual non-unique witnesses.


7     From first-order rigidity to multiplicity bounds
A full-rank pointwise result does not imply uniqueness. The simplest counterexample is w2 = x.
To distinguish “one value” from “finitely many values,” an additional degree argument is needed.

7.1   Triangular degree certificates
The safest setting is a triangular subsystem in which variables can be introduced one at a time.

Definition 11 (Triangular certificate). Fix the conditioned coordinates. A triangular certificate
for variables w1 , . . . , wt consists of polynomials

                     g1 (w1 ) = 0,   g2 (w1 , w2 ) = 0,   ...,   gt (w1 , . . . , wt ) = 0,


                                                    10
each belonging to the conditioned constraint ideal and involving only w1 , . . . , wi , such that for every
solution of the preceding equations over Fp , the polynomial gi (w1 , . . . , wi−1 , ·) is nonzero and has
degree at most di . An elimination or substitution step is admissible only when the relation used is
itself entailed by the constraint ideal.

Proposition 12 (Product-of-degrees bound). Under a triangular certificate as above, the number
of solutions over Fp is at most

The number of Fp -rational solutions is therefore at most the same quantity.

Proof. For each fixed prefix (w1 , . . . , wi−1 ), the next nonzero univariate equation has at most di
roots over Fp . Induction over the chain gives the product bound.

    The per-constraint step of this bound—a wire presented as a degree-d univariate polynomial
takes at most d values, and d = 1 recovers determinacy—is machine-checked in Lean (Section 11.4);
the composition into a product over a chain is a pen-and-paper bound and is not formally verified.
    For an R1CS chain, each original constraint has total degree at most two. If the triangular
certificate uses original constraints in a way that introduces exactly one new variable per step and
preserves a nonzero leading coeﬀicient, then each di ≤ 2 and

where q is the number of genuinely quadratic steps. Linear steps contribute a factor of one.

7.2   Why the 2q bound is conditional
The qualification above is essential. General elimination can raise degrees even when every input
constraint is quadratic. Cycles, shared unknowns, vanishing leading coeﬀicients, positive- dimen-
sional components, and hidden elimination polynomials can all invalidate a naive count based on
the number of syntactically quadratic constraints in a dependency cone. Consequently, the imple-
mentation should emit a multiplicity bound only together with a structural certificate that justifies
the chosen triangular order. Otherwise the result is unknown, not 2q .
    The coupled system
                                      w + u = 5,      wu = 6
illustrates both sides. A purely syntactic rule looking for w2 misses the ambiguity, but the ideal
combination
                             w(w + u − 5) − (wu − 6) = w2 − 5w + 6
provides a valid certificate polynomial in w alone; the original linear equation then fixes u. The
resulting multiplicity bound is 2 · 1 = 2.

7.3   Relation to Bézout bounds
Classical Bézout bounds provide a more general route to bounding isolated solutions, but they are
typically too coarse for circuit diagnosis and require hypotheses about dimension and components.
The triangular product is attractive because the certificate is local, auditable, and naturally aligned
with circuit structure. It should be viewed as a refinement layer on top of the Jacobian analysis,
not as a complete multiplicity algorithm.

8     Beyond R1CS: PLONKish arithmetizations
Nothing in the pointwise construction is specific to R1CS. The tangent-space identity (Proposition 9)
and the row-space test (Corollary 10) use only that the constraints are polynomials vanishing at
the sampled witness, so they transfer verbatim to any polynomial arithmetization. In a PLONKish
system the coordinates are the cells of the execution trace, one per (column, row). Each gate
instance is a polynomial in those cells and contributes its differential row to J(a) directly; this
includes higher-degree custom gates and gates that couple several rows through rotations, since a
rotation is only a reference to a cell in another row. Public and fixed cells are pinned by EF as
before. Copy (permutation) constraints are linear equalities xa = xb , so their differentials are the
constant, witness-independent rows e⊤             ⊤

in the quotient that identifies copy-equal cells—the PLONK notion of a wire. Selectors are fixed
columns rather than prover-controlled cells, so the conditional-freedom phenomenon of Section 5
can be driven only by advice cells, never by a chosen selector.

work. The same remarks apply to any arithmetization with an execution trace and transition or
boundary polynomials, such as AIR, where rotations again reduce to references between rows.


9     Witness locality
9.1   A pointwise matrix describes one witness
The matrix M (a) depends on a. Changing the witness can change coeﬀicients in the Jacobian and
therefore change its rank and nullspace. There are three distinct reasons.

1. Special or singular points can lose rank. The equation w2 = 0 has derivative zero at
   its only solution, producing a tangent direction that does not correspond to another reduced
   solution.


                                                     12
2. Finite ambiguities can be locally rigid. In w2 = 1, both roots have zero tangent freedom
   even though the fibre contains two points.

3. Conditional constraints can change rank across branches. A guard or hint verification
   equation can be binding on an honest branch and vacuous on a degenerate branch.

    The first issue produces false positives if rank deficiency is interpreted as non-uniqueness. The
second and third produce false negatives if first-order rigidity at one witness is interpreted as global
uniqueness.

9.4    Adversarial witness generation
For security use, witness generation should therefore be treated as part of the analysis rather than
as a neutral preprocessing step. For hint-based or conditionally verified gadgets, useful witness
families include

• all-zero hint outputs;

• zero and boundary scalars;

• identity or exceptional group elements;

• selector values on both sides of a guard;

• range boundaries and values immediately outside an intended range when they remain field-
  satisfiable;

• denominator-zero or inverse-zero branches;

• values that collapse two nominally distinct intermediate quantities.

   This is not the same as drawing a random honest witness. Sampling additional satisfying wit-
nesses can help reveal conclusions that depend on a special point, but an ambient-space Schwartz–
Zippel argument does not justify such sampling: the analysis is restricted to the circuit variety,
and an honest witness generator follows program semantics rather than a uniform distribution on
that variety. It can therefore systematically avoid precisely the satisfying assignments available to
a malicious prover through unconstrained hints.

9.5    Case splitting is relocated
The Jacobian computation itself does not symbolically split on selectors. Once a witness is fixed,
guards, masks, and selects are ordinary field coeﬀicients in a sparse matrix. This is a genuine com-
putational advantage. It should not be stated as elimination of case analysis for the whole security

                                                      14
problem. If different prover-reachable branches have different ranks, representative witnesses for
those branches must still be generated. The case analysis has moved from nonlinear constraint
solving to witness selection.
    For many practical gadgets this relocation is useful because the set of security-relevant degenera-
cies is small and structured. The resulting workflow is closer to targeted adversarial test generation
followed by exact algebraic diagnosis than to a global decision procedure.


10 Sound interpretation of results
A useful implementation should expose the type of statement established rather than placing all
outputs on one numerical scale. The following result classes are not a hierarchy; in particular,
component-wise algebraic freedom and finite algebraic dependence describe different branches of
the geometry.

Pointwise infinitesimal freedom.
    A nullspace vector has a nonzero target coordinate. This is an exact statement about the
    sampled fibre scheme at the sampled witness.

Component/generic algebraic freedom.
   Additional component and genericity analysis shows that the target lies outside the algebraic-
   matroid closure of the fixed coordinates. This establishes generic transcendence on that com-
   ponent but does not produce two Fp witnesses.

Finite-dependence or multiplicity certificate.
    A triangular or elimination certificate proves algebraic dependence and may bound the number
    of possible values. A bound greater than one is only an upper bound.

Concrete finite-field non-uniqueness certificate.
   Two satisfying assignments agree on the public statement and structural constants and differ
   on a security-relevant target. This directly establishes non-uniqueness.

    Conversely, a pointwise “rigid” result should never be labelled safe. The appropriate wording
is “no first-order freedom found at the tested witness.” A global safety claim requires a separate
proof or sound uniqueness checker.


11 Toward certificates beyond pointwise rank
The gap between a local diagnostic and a global proof suggests several ways to combine methods.

11.1   Second-witness construction
The most direct confirmation is to use the Jacobian result to identify a small suspicious cone and
ask a solver for a second witness there. All public coordinates and all boundary wires imported
from outside the slice must remain fixed, and every original constraint whose support meets a
modified wire must be included. Any candidate must then be spliced back into the full assignment
and rechecked against the complete R1CS, with a final check that a security-relevant target changes.
Those full-system checks make the counterexample globally sound while reserving nonlinear solving
for the suspicious region.


                                                  15
11.2   Elimination and ideal membership
For a target xj , one can ask whether the elimination ideal on the public variables and xj contains
a polynomial that is linear in xj . A relation

                                       A(xP )xj − B(xP ) = 0

with A(u) ̸= 0 proves uniqueness of xj at the fixed public statement u within the component or va-
riety covered by the certificate. More general elimination polynomials give multiplicity information
through their degree in xj .
    Computing such certificates globally can be much more expensive than Jacobian rank. The
pointwise analysis is valuable precisely because it can identify a small set of targets and constraints
for which stronger algebraic work is justified.

11.3   Radical and component issues
The w2 = 0 example shows why non-radical generators matter. A complete algebraic treatment
would work with the radical ideal and, for algebraic-matroid statements, with its prime components.
Full primary decomposition is not a plausible preprocessing step for large ZK circuits. Practical
analysis therefore needs cheaper surrogates: repeated witnesses, local smoothness checks, syntactic
recognition of common square/zero patterns, or certificate generation only on small suspicious
slices.

11.4   A machine-checked determinacy certificate
For the wires the pointwise test reports as rigid, determinacy can be confirmed—soundly, and
independently of the rank computation—by a small machine-checked checker. We have formalised
in Lean 4 (against mathlib, with no sorry and only the standard axioms) a fold-based determinacy
certificate checker: generic soundness theorems for functional, is-zero, guarded-quotient, and bit-
decomposition constraint shapes are proved once, and an assume–guarantee composition theorem
stitches the per-leaf facts into “every output is determined by the inputs.” A generated certificate
for a concrete circuit is then discharged by data plus one decidable evaluation. This is a complement
to, not a formalisation of, the Jacobian: it certifies determinacy from structural constraint shapes
rather than computing an algebraic rank, and its guarded rules carry an explicit divisor-nonzero
side condition. It occupies the sound end of the interpretation spectrum of Section 10—where the
Jacobian offers a fast local signal, the checker offers a machine-checked determinacy guarantee for
the shapes it recognises.


12 Evaluation methodology
A full empirical evaluation should separate performance from semantic effectiveness. The following
research questions capture the distinction.

RQ1: Does the implementation compute the intended linear-algebraic object? For
every benchmark witness, the tool should first verify all R1CS constraints. Sparse rank results
should be cross-checked against an independent exact implementation on instances that fit both
paths. Small hand-constructed systems should cover bilinear freedom, guards, square-root ambigu-
ity, non-radical singularities, and coupled finite solutions.



                                                  16
RQ2: How does exact Jacobian processing scale? Report constraints, wires, Jacobian
nonzeros, peak memory, wall-clock time, fill-in, and rank for each benchmark. Dense and sparse
paths should be compared only where both complete. The current prototype already reaches 6k–60k
constraints with an observed 500–1000× improvement over the dense implementation; publication-
quality results should include the complete benchmark matrix and pinned hardware/software ver-
sions.

RQ3: How often do pointwise candidates correspond to real non-uniqueness? For
each flagged target, attempt to construct or solve for a second satisfying witness. Report true
counterexamples separately from singular/non-radical false alarms and from cases left unresolved.
This measures diagnostic precision rather than merely rank deficiency.

RQ4: How sensitive are results to witness selection? For branch-heavy and hint-heavy
gadgets, evaluate the same compiled R1CS at honest, randomised, and adversarially constructed
satisfying witnesses. Table 2 is one instance of this experiment. The important outcome is the
delta in target freedom across witness families.

RQ5: What does multiplicity analysis add? On targets that are first-order rigid, attempt
to derive triangular degree certificates. Report how many targets receive bounds 1, 2, 4, and so on,
and how often the structural check must return unknown. This directly tests whether the degree
layer separates benign local rigidity from finite ambiguity in practice.

13 A public soundness benchmark and an applicability taxonomy
The reach and the limits of the method are both sharpened by a public corpus. A critical advi-
sory for the gnark standard library (eleven soundness issues, fixed in release 0.16.2) collects real,
independently discovered defects in emulated-field arithmetic, pairing, and elliptic-curve scalar-
multiplication gadgets. Because it was not designed around any detector, it is a fair external test
of what a first-order Jacobian diagnostic does and does not see.

assignments—a sign, a root, or an alternative sub-scalar decomposition—each first-order rigid, so
rank misses them at any single witness (the w2 = x phenomenon of Section 5); the triangular degree

14 Related work
Uniqueness checking for ZK circuits. Pailoor et al. introduce QED2 , implemented in Picus,
which combines uniqueness-constraint propagation with SMT queries and returns verified, refuted,
or unknown results [1]. Its security property is global and relational: two assignments with the same



                                                  18
input witness non-uniqueness. At the solver level, subsequent work develops dedicated reasoning
for integer constraints modulo different constants arising in cryptographic verification [3].
    Soureshjani et al. analyse Halo2 circuits using abstract interpretation for structural properties
and SMT for under-constraint checks [2].

Direct algebraic solving. AC4 translates circuit constraints into polynomial systems over finite
fields and uses algebraic computation to classify circuit behaviour [4]. The present work is com-
plementary: rather than solving the system, it evaluates its differential linearisation at selected
satisfying points.

Fuzzing and computation–constraint consistency. zkFuzz introduces the Trace-Constraint
Consistency Test, a broader computation–constraint consistency property covering both under-
and over-constrained behaviour, and searches for violations using program mutation [5]. It was
published at IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2026. These methods address witness and
execution exploration directly.

Elliptic-curve gadget soundness. Concurrent work on SNARK soundness has also targeted
elliptic-curve gadgets. El Housni [11] shows that gnark’s hinted scalar-multiplication gadgets are
unsound on cofactor curves because the hinted output is never constrained into the prime-order
subgroup, and constructs cofactor-torsion forgeries on BLS12-381, BW6-761, and BN254. That
work is a cryptographic attack and fix by manual analysis—its bug is off-model group torsion that
leaves the R1CS fully determined—whereas we give an automated Jacobian/rank-based method
for detecting under-constrained signals. The two are complementary: torsion soundness gaps of
that kind are precisely the semantic omissions our field-level analysis does not capture (Section 13),
delimiting our scope rather than overlapping it.

Algebraic independence and algebraic matroids. The Jacobian criterion for algebraic inde-
pendence is classical. Beecken, Mittmann, and Saxena give large-characteristic criteria [7]; Agrawal,
Saha, Saptharishi, and Saxena use Jacobians in polynomial identity testing and lower bounds [8].
Positive characteristic requires care; Pandey, Saxena, and Sinhababu develop a criterion for this
regime [9]. Rosen, Sidman, and Theran give a modern account of algebraic matroids and differ-
ential representations [6]. The implementation here is a pointwise sparse-Jacobian diagnostic; the
algebraic-matroid language supplies its generic component-wise interpretation rather than a claim
that the tool computes prime decompositions or algebraic matroids globally.


15 Limitations
The method has several limitations that should remain explicit in any security use.

1. Pointwise rather than global. The Jacobian at a describes first-order behaviour at a. It
   does not quantify over all satisfying witnesses.

2. Finite ambiguity is invisible to rank alone. Isolated alternative roots can have full local
   rank at every root.

3. Non-radical ideals and singular points create false alarms. Scheme-theoretic tangent
   directions need not correspond to distinct reduced solutions.


                                                 19
 4. Reducible varieties are component-sensitive. Algebraic matroids are naturally defined
    on irreducible components. A witness on one component says nothing about a disconnected
    component not sampled.

 5. Fp geometry is not identical to Fp security. Algebraic dependence and geometric dimension
    are naturally stated over an algebraic closure. Actual circuit witnesses live in Fp . A geometric
    candidate may require a separate finite-field witness construction.

 6. Multiplicity bounds require certificates. The 2q rule is sound only for a verified triangular
    chain with nonvanishing leading coeﬀicients; it is not valid for an arbitrary quadratic cone.

 7. Witness generation is part of the threat model. Honest solvers can systematically avoid
    prover-steerable degenerate branches. Security analysis must include adversarial witnesses.

 8. The target set is semantic. Linear algebra cannot determine which internal wires matter to
    the intended application relation. That mapping still requires compiler metadata, specification,
    or manual review.

 9. Whole-circuit separability is not guaranteed by quadratic syntax. The degree-budget
    certificate in Corollary 8 is suﬀicient at gadget scale, but beyond it the Frobenius-chain example
    shows that ordinary differentials can fail even when every individual constraint is quadratic.

10. The current empirical evidence is preliminary. The speedup figures do not yet have
    complete per-instance reproducibility metadata. The witness-locality case study, by contrast,
    is fully reproducible from public gnark 0.14.0 source.

11. Semantic completeness of the constraint model. The analysis reasons only about the
    polynomial relation represented by the compiled R1CS. It cannot detect a defect for which that
    relation is itself a faithful, fully determined polynomial system but omits an external semantic
    invariant. For example, subgroup or cofactor conditions on elliptic-curve points may distinguish
    [s]P from [s]P + T even when the accepted R1CS assignment is locally and globally determined
    over the circuit field. Such failures are outside the model rather than false negatives of Jacobian
    rank.

   These limitations do not negate the scale advantage. They determine how the result should be
used: as an inexpensive algebraic lens that narrows the search space for stronger analyses.


16 Practical audit workflow
For circuit auditing, the following workflow has worked better than treating the Jacobian as a
stand-alone verifier.

 1. Identify public statement coordinates and security-relevant targets from the intended relation.

 2. Compile the exact in-scope circuit and export an honest satisfying witness.

 3. Run the sparse pointwise analysis and rank targets by nullspace support; record whether Corol-
    lary 8 certifies separability for each analysed cone.

 4. Generate adversarial witnesses for hints, selectors, exceptional group elements, inverse checks,
    and range boundaries; rerun the same matrix analysis on each.


                                                  20
5. For every security-relevant target exposed by any witness, slice the relevant dependency cone.

6. Attempt concrete second-witness construction or a solver-based relational check on the slice.

7. For locally rigid but suspicious targets, attempt a triangular degree certificate or targeted
   elimination to bound finite ambiguity.

8. Report the strongest established statement: pointwise freedom, multiplicity bound, or actual
   second-witness counterexample. Do not promote a local rigid verdict to global safety.

   This division of labour is useful because each technique is applied where it is strongest. Sparse
rank handles large systems cheaply; adversarial witness generation explores conditional behaviour;
and expensive symbolic reasoning is reserved for small, security-relevant slices.


17 Conclusion
Under-constraint is not a single algebraic property. The security question is usually uniqueness of
selected values over the circuit field after fixing the public statement. Algebraic-matroid closure
captures a weaker, generic finite-dependence property on an irreducible component. A Jacobian at
one witness captures a still more local first-order property. Keeping these notions separate turns
the Jacobian from an overclaimed decision procedure into a precise and useful diagnostic.
    For R1CS, the diagnostic is particularly inexpensive. The derivative rows are explicit and
sparse, public inputs are fixed by adding coordinate rows, and exact nullspace information can be
computed by finite-field linear algebra. The current implementation reaches tens of thousands of
constraints, and preliminary measurements show substantial speedups over its dense predecessor on
the tested instances. On guarded and bilinear patterns it identifies coupled local freedom without
symbolic case splitting inside the matrix computation.
    The main obstacle is witness locality. A circuit can be rigid at an honest witness and under-
constrained on a prover-reachable degenerate branch. The measured hint-based case study demon-
strates that this is not merely a theoretical qualification. Accordingly, the most promising ar-
chitecture is hybrid: adversarial witness generation to explore branch-sensitive behaviour, sparse
Jacobian analysis to localise freedom, and solver- or certificate-based reasoning to establish actual
non-uniqueness or uniqueness where the security claim requires it.
